title: House Robber
description: Max sum of non-adjacent elements. At each house: rob (prev2 + n) or skip (prev1). Classic 1D DP with O(1) rolling scalars.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm given an array of non-negative integers where each entry is the cash in a house on a street. I'm picking houses to rob, but I can't rob two adjacent ones — the alarm goes off. I want the maximum total I can carry out."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Are values strictly non-negative, or can they be zero/negative?
• Empty array — return 0?
• Single house — just return `nums[0]`?
• Return value — just the max sum, or also the indices I robbed?
• Can I assume the input fits in memory? Any bound on length?
sections.why: The non-negative question matters because the recurrence relies on 'taking more is never worse' — if values could be negative, the skip-vs-rob comparison still works but the framing changes (you'd never voluntarily rob a negative house, but the structure stays the same). Confirming the empty and single-element cases pins down the base seeds: `prev2 = prev1 = 0` covers both.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(2^n) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is exponential recursion: at each house I have two choices — skip it (move to `i+1` with the same haul) or rob it (move to `i+2` adding `nums[i]`). Return the max of the two subtrees. That's `O(2^n)` time because every house branches in two, with massive overlap — `rob(i)` from skipping `i-1` and `rob(i)` from robbing `i-2`-then-skipping-`i-1` both compute the same subproblem."
sections.why: Naming the two recursive branches — skip vs rob — out loud is what plants the recurrence. The DP cell is literally `max(skip-branch, rob-branch)`. Saying it as recursion first makes the bottom-up version a translation, not a leap. The overlap is also what justifies switching to DP rather than just memoizing the recursion.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to 1D DP with rolling variables?
sections.say: "This is a 1D DP. The recurrence is `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i])` — at each house I'm making one binary decision: skip (so my best is whatever I had at `i-1`) or rob (so my best is whatever I had at `i-2` plus this house, because robbing `i` forbids `i-1`). The adjacency constraint is exactly what reaches back two cells instead of one. And because `dp[i]` only reads `dp[i-1]` and `dp[i-2]`, the full array is unnecessary — two rolling scalars `prev2` and `prev1` are enough. Time O(n), space O(1)."
sections.why: Articulating the decision *and* the constraint that creates the look-back is the move. 'Skip vs rob' alone is incomplete; 'skip vs rob, and rob forbids the immediate predecessor, which is why we reach back to `i-2`' is the full derivation. That's the same shape as Climbing Stairs (Fibonacci-style look-back of 2), just with a max-with-payload instead of a sum.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a typical mix where skip wins twice, a case where skip-then-rob beats every greedy strategy, and the single-house degenerate.

examples.note: Canonical case — optimal is rob(2) + rob(9) + rob(1) = 12.
examples.trace:
init: prev2=0, prev1=0
i=0 n=2: curr = max(skip=0, rob=0+2=2) = 2. roll → (0,2). dp[0]=2
i=1 n=7: curr = max(skip=2, rob=0+7=7) = 7. roll → (2,7). dp[1]=7
i=2 n=9: curr = max(skip=7, rob=2+9=11) = 11. roll → (7,11). dp[2]=11
i=3 n=3: curr = max(skip=11, rob=7+3=10) = 11. roll → (11,11). dp[3]=11
i=4 n=1: curr = max(skip=11, rob=11+1=12) = 12. roll → (11,12). dp[4]=12
return 12

examples.note: Skip-then-rob beats greedy — robbing 2 at the start AND 2 at the end (skipping the middle) totals 4, better than any other plan.
Single house — the loop runs once and the seed `prev2 = 0` makes rob the obvious winner.
examples.trace:
init: prev2=0, prev1=0
i=0 n=5: curr = max(skip=0, rob=0+5=5) = 5. roll → (0,5). dp[0]=5
return 5

sections.why: Tracing surfaces two things. (1) The roll order — assign `prev2 = prev1` BEFORE `prev1 = curr`, or you stomp the value you still need to read next iteration. (2) The `[2,1,1,2]` case shows why greedy 'always rob the biggest available' fails: greedy picks 2 then 1 = 3, but skip-then-rob picks 2 and 2 = 4. That trace defends *why* this needs DP and not a simple scan.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• `[]` — loop doesn't run, `prev1 = 0` returned. ✓
• `[5]` — loop runs once, `max(0, 0+5) = 5`. ✓
• `[5, 10]` — two houses, can only rob one; result should be max(5, 10) = 10. Trace: `max(0, 0+5)=5`, then `max(5, 0+10)=10`. ✓
• All zeros — every iteration computes `max(0, 0+0) = 0`. Returns 0. ✓
• Strictly increasing — every decision favors robbing the latest, because skipping the previous unlocks more. The recurrence still handles it correctly; no special case needed.
• Very large values — sums of integers can overflow JS's safe integer range if values are near `2^53`; switch to BigInt if that's in play."
sections.why: Walking through the small-array cases on the same recurrence shows the loop's invariant works without any if-branches for small inputs — that's a senior signal. Most candidates write `if (n === 0) return 0; if (n === 1) return nums[0];` guards as defensive programming, then realize the rolling-vars version handles both implicitly. The overflow note is the bonus that flags data-type awareness.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — one pass through the array, constant work per house (one max, one add, two assignments). Space is O(1) — just the two scalars `prev2` and `prev1`, no array allocation.

The naive recursion was O(2^n) time; memoization brings it to O(n) time / O(n) space; tabulation stays at O(n) / O(n); rolling pair drops space to O(1). Same trajectory as Climbing Stairs.

For the natural follow-up: House Robber II (houses arranged in a circle, so houses 0 and n-1 are now adjacent) — you run House Robber twice: once on `nums[0..n-2]`, once on `nums[1..n-1]`, take the max. Same template, just split the input two ways to break the circular constraint. House Robber III is the tree variant — same skip-vs-rob recurrence, recursed down a binary tree."
sections.why: The 2^n → n → 1 space progression is the right defense — interviewers love seeing you understand *why* each step works (overlapping subproblems → memo, limited look-back → rolling vars). The House Robber II/III extensions prove you see the template as 'skip-vs-take with constraint on adjacency' rather than this one problem; that same shape recurs in Delete and Earn, Paint House, and any 'partition with non-adjacency' problem.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the rolling-pair House Robber on real inputs. Each iteration decides skip-vs-rob; the synthetic dp array shows the running best at every prefix.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — nums=${JSON.stringify(nums)}`, state: { nums } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init prev2=0, prev1=0 (no houses robbed yet)', state: { nums, prev2, prev1, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 5, label: `outer step: i=${i}, house value=${n}`, state: { nums, i, n, prev2, prev1, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 6, label: `curr = max(skip=${prev1}, rob=${prev2}+${n}=${prev2 + n}) = ${curr}`, state: { nums, i, n, prev2, prev1, curr, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 8, label: `roll: prev2 = prev1 = ${prev2}`, state: { nums, i, n, prev2, prev1, curr, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 9, label: `roll: prev1 = curr = ${prev1} — dp[${i}]=${curr} filled`, state: { nums, i, n, prev2, prev1, dp: [...dp], lastFilled: i } };
yield { line: 11, label: `return prev1 = ${prev1}`, state: { nums, prev2, prev1, dp: [...dp], returns: prev1 } };

notes: Recurrence: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]) — either skip i or take i and lose i-1.
Both bases are 0 (no houses robbed yet); prev1 ends up holding the answer.
Update order matters — assign prev2 = prev1 BEFORE prev1 = curr, or you overwrite the value you still need.
reference.crux: At each house, skip it (keep dp[i-1]) or rob it (dp[i-2] + nums[i], since robbing forbids the neighbor): dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).
cruxDistractors: Greedily rob the largest available house, then skip its two neighbors and repeat — fails on [2,1,1,2] (picks 2+1=3, misses 2+2=4).
Sum every other house and take the larger of the two alternating sets (even indices vs odd indices).
dp[i] = max(dp[i-1] + nums[i], dp[i-2]) — adds the current house to the adjacent total, violating the no-adjacent rule.

alternates.label: Explicit dp array (O(n) space)
alternates.when: Reach for this when an interviewer wants to see the dp table before the space compression. Makes it easy to walk through the table and explain dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]) cell by cell before the rolling-pair shortcut.
notes: dp[1] is seeded as max(nums[0], nums[1]) — the best of the first two houses, since you can only pick one of them.
Each dp[i] records the optimal haul over the first (i+1) houses; the rolling-pair collapses this to just two scalars.
Transition to O(1): note dp[i] reads only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] — identical to the climbing-stairs rolling-pair pattern.

questions.q: The recurrence for House Robber is:
Why cannot we rob two adjacent houses?
options: Because the recurrence dp[i] = dp[i-1] + nums[i] would create overlapping subproblems
Problem constraint — adjacent houses trigger the alarm
Because robbing two adjacent houses is provably never optimal (their sum is dominated by skip-then-rob on three consecutive cells)
Because the rolling-pair invariant requires a one-cell gap between picks for prev2 to stay independent
